newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-Campbell's new CEO sees marketing focus.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Campbell's new CEO sees marketing focus.

text.p: Campbell Soup Co's newly appointed president and chief executive, Dale Morrison, plans to stick with the company's existing strategic plan for boosting sales and earnings growth, which places a strong emphasis on increased advertising.

Morrison, named Monday to succeed David Johnson in the posts, said in an interview he aimed to increase marketing spending on Campbell's core soup line and pursue international acquisitions as part of a strategy to fuel growth. Johnson will remain the company's chairman.

Morrison forecast an increase of "30 percent plus" in U.S. spending to support soups in fiscal 1997-98, which begins in August. The marketing drive would also involve expanding the presence of Campbell's soups in places such as convenience stores and airports, he said.

In addition, Robert Bernstock, president of Campbell's core U.S. grocery division, has indicated he will remain at the company with his elevated title of executive vice president, Morrison said. Bernstock was regarded as a contender for the chief executive slot.

Referring to his strategy as president and chief executive, Morrison said, "The September (1996) strategic growth plan is our road map. I don't see that changing." He will take over the posts on July 15.
That plan aims to improve earnings by 14 to 16 percent a year through 1999, while increasing annual sales growth to around eight percent from existing rates of three to four percent a year.
Cost savings from job reductions and restructuring would in part help finance increased marketing spending.
Morrison said the company was on track to meet the 14 percent earnings growth target for fiscal 1996-97, which ends in July. He declined to comment on later years.

Discussing the sales growth goals, he said, "We've had a wonderful few years on Wall Street. Our market value has tripled since 1990, and now we need to do a better job of winning on Main Street, of winning with consumers," he said.

He said he was confident of showing sales growth in the U.S. soup market, which Campbell already dominates, by expanding "soup relevance" to consumers, innovation in products such as premium soups and increased availability.

"You don't just have to go to the grocery store to buy soup....Campbell's Soup should be available and should be in arm's reach of desire, whether that be in airports or convenience stores or wherever."

Bernstock's continued presence at Campbell, where he oversees operations responsible for more than half the company's profits, is regarded by analysts as important for Campbell's future. "He has said very openly that he's staying," Morrison said.
Acquisitions, especially international, would be "an important piilar" of the growth plan, Morrison said.
